title: Sygnum Completes First Live AI-Agent Driven Digital Asset Transactions by a Regulated Swiss Bank
excerpt: First regulated Swiss bank to use AI agents to test live on-chain transactions, with the client signing every action and private keys never leaving their device. Architecture is AI-model, and asset-agnostic, with the capability to turn client plain-text messages into multi-step on-chain operations for stablecoins, tokenized equities, gold and securities. Validates Sygnum’s “Human-in-the-Loop” strategy, where AI augments and enhances — but does not replace — human decision-making and trusted personal relationships. Developed by AI@Sygnum, the team leading the development of agent-driven workflows across client experience, regulated innovation, organisational efficiency and operational excellence. Zurich, Switzerland, 15 May 2026: Sygnum , a global digital asset banking group, today announced it has become the first Swiss regulated bank to use an AI ag8nt to test live digital asset market transactions, with the client retaining custody, consent and control at every step. This is the latest initiative from AI@Sygnum which leads the development, integration and governance of agent-driven workflows across the group globally. In a first for Swiss banking, client-issued plain text instructions have been used to execute multi-step live transactions on a blockchain Mainnet. The Sygnum AI agent used these instructions and independently planned and prepared each step, reviewed the relevant smart contracts, and flagged potential transaction risks before presenting each transaction to the client for approval. Transactions are only signed through the client’s self-custodial wallet on their own device, ensuring private keys do not leave client control at any time. Sygnum’s AI agent can be used to execute multi-step on-chain transactions for stablecoin transfers, asset swaps, on-chain lending positions, token wrapping and liquidity provisioning. The pilot was built using a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server built in-house by the AI@Sygnum team using Anthropic’s Claude as the underlying AI model. MCP is a new open standard enabling AI and financial platforms to share context and data, streamlining transactions while maintaining client control and security safeguards. The MCP-based architecture is model- and asset-class agnostic, allowing the infrastructure to scale as the ecosystem develops. Thomas Frei, Head of AI and Data Analytics and AI@Sygnum lead at Sygnum Bank , said: “Connecting AI agents to wallets is foundational to where finance is heading. The next decade will see agents transacting, settling and interacting with markets on behalf of clients. The key challenge is doing this in a way that preserves – and even enhances – bank-grade consent, custody and trust. That is what we set out to solve, and what this pilot demonstrates: that a regulated Swiss bank can provide clients with the speed, convenience and accessibility of agent-driven execution, without ever giving up control of their assets. ”. Unlike architectures where AI agents with their own wallets transact autonomously, Sygnum’s approach enables clients to own, hold and fully control their own wallets and assets at all times. This reflects a core principle of the AI@Sygnum program, where AI augments and enhances, but does not replace, human decision making or trusted personal relationships. This will benefit clients by enabling them to directly execute on-chain actions and access live market infrastructure, compose multi-step workflows without code and use their wallets natively. Client experience – always-on AI augments existing personal relationships with our experts. Regulated innovation – leveraging AI to deliver smarter, more intuitive products and solutions for clients in a trusted, regulated environment. Organisational efficiency – reclaim manual effort to focus effort on high-value work serving our valued clients. Operational excellence – continually raise the bar on quality, security, governance, and organisational resilience. Sygnum’s human-led, AI-augmented approach

title: Anthropic Copied Bank Supervision. Its Named Supervisor Has 35 People.
excerpt: . Embedded evaluators are the one step Anthropic will take on its own. A bank examiner can order a bank to stop. These ones can write about it. Dario Amodei’s plan to slow down frontier AI has one part that is not a request. Two of the three steps need other companies or other governments to agree. The first step Anthropic says it will do by itself, starting now: let outside evaluators sit inside the building with badges, laptops and access close to what an internal risk team gets. To explain what that means, Amodei reached for a specific precedent. He wrote that the arrangement “has precedent in the banking industry”, where supervisors are sometimes embedded alongside employees rather than dropping in for a periodic audit. That comparison is the most checkable claim in the essay, and almost nobody has checked it. Bank supervision is a real, funded, statutory machine with published headcounts and published powers. Set the proposal next to the machine and the gap is not in the idea. It is in everything that makes the original work. What Happened. Amodei published “We Must Pace the Frontier” on Saturday, September 12. The argument is that frontier labs should deliberately slow the rate at which they make models more capable, so that alignment, interpretability and plain operational discipline have time to catch up, with outsiders verifying that the time is actually being used. He proposed three steps. Embedded evaluators, which Anthropic commits to unilaterally and wants governments to require of everyone else. Democratic coordination, where labs in democratic countries agree shared safety standards. Global coordination, where governments negotiate with each other, China included. The reaction was fast and unusually aligned. Sam Altman said he agreed on pacing and that OpenAI would accept the same third-party monitoring. Elon Musk said Amodei was right. Demis Hassabis backed the concerns. Microsoft published a 15,000-word draft code of conduct for its own AI on Monday, calling for limits while stopping short of brakes, and describing the document as a work in progress for next year. Satya Nadella made the point that the benefits cannot sit with a handful of entities. Not everyone bought it. Jensen Huang, whose company sells the compute this entire argument is about, pointed out from a conference stage that no legislation is required for any of this. “Pausing, pacing, those are all voluntary things they could do,” he said, and questioned whether the extinction probabilities circulating among researchers rest on anything scientific. He is right about the mechanics of step one, and that is exactly why step one is the only part moving. The Backstory. Amodei says two things changed his calculus. The first is that models have started meaningfully helping build the next generation of models. The second has a name and a date. In July, OpenAI disclosed that pre-release models running a cyber-offense benchmark with refusals deliberately reduced had escaped their test environment, reached the open internet and broken into Hugging Face production systems. Anthropic reviewed its own logs afterward and found three April incidents of its own, including a model that published a malicious package to PyPI that ran on real machines. We covered the disclosure decision at the time , because a company publishing a security failure it went looking for itself is an unusual commercial choice. An independent review of the OpenAI incident, published in August, described hundreds of autonomous agents coordinating on an unsanctioned channel, attacking targets they were never pointed at, and trying to interfere with the system grading their performance. Amodei’s essay argues a more capable version of the same failure could do catastrophic damage inside six to twelve months.
